column2: Struck by the king of the Madras' mace, Bhima's mace, as if blazing, sent forth flames of fire, O king.
So too Shalya's mace, struck by Bhima's mace, rained sparks; it was as marvellous.
As two great elephants with tusks, as two great bulls with horns, as with goads, they struck each other then with their maces' points.
Their bodies struck by maces, quickly smeared with blood, they became yet more beautiful to behold, like two flowering kimshuka trees.
Struck right and left by the king of the Madras' mace, the mighty-armed Bhimasena did not move, like a mountain.
So too, being struck again and again by the force of Bhima's mace, Shalya was not pained, O king, like a mountain struck by an elephant.
In all quarters was heard the crash of the falling maces of those two lions among men, like the roar of thunderbolts.
Turning back, those two of great valour, with maces raised, stood again in the middle of the way and ranged in circles.
Then, advancing eight paces, a clash took place between them, raising their iron clubs, of superhuman deed.
Wishing to reach each other, they ranged in circles, and those two skilled ones showed special feats then.
Then, raising their dreadful maces, like two mountains with peaks, they struck each other, as two mountains in an earthquake.
By the force of each other and struck hard by the maces, the two heroes fell at once, like two banners of Indra.
A cry of "Alas" arose among the heroes of both armies; both lay struck in their vitals, greatly bewildered.
Then Kripa placed the bull of the Madras with his mace on his chariot and quickly carried Shalya away from the battlefield.
Bewildered as if drunk, he rose again after a moment; Bhimasena, mace in hand, challenged the lord of the Madras.
Then your brave men, armed with weapons of many kinds and with the sounds of many instruments, fought the Pandava army.
Raising their arms and weapons with a great noise, led by Duryodhana, O great king, they rushed on.
Seeing that division, the sons of Pandu advanced with a lion-roar, wishing to slay Duryodhana.
As they swiftly came on, your son, O best of the Bharatas, pierced Chekitana hard in the heart with a lance.
Struck by your son, he fell on the chariot seat, drenched in floods of blood, entering a vast darkness.
Seeing Chekitana slain, the great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas continuously showered by portions showers of arrows.
Among your divisions the victorious Pandavas ranged, O great king, a sight to behold on every side.
Kripa, Kritavarman and the mighty son of Subala, putting the king of the Madras in front, fought the king of dharma.
Duryodhana, O great king, fought Dhrishtadyumna, slayer of Bharadvaja's son, of great valour.
Three thousand chariots urged by your son, O king, fought for victory with Drona's son put in front.
Resolved on victory, having abandoned life, your men entered, O king, like swans a great lake.
Then a dreadful battle took place of those wishing each other's death, bound to mutual slaughter, increasing mutual delight.
While that battle went on, O king, with the destruction of great heroes, a dreadful dust of the earth rose, driven by wind.
From the proclaiming of names of warriors, and the Pandavas, we recognised one another, and those who fought fearlessly.
That dust, tiger among men, was quenched by blood, and with the dust quenched the quarters became clear.
While that dreadful, terrible battle went on, none among yours or the enemy's was turned away.
Intent on the world of Brahma, seeking victory in battle, men valiant in good fighting, desiring heaven,
to repay their master's food, resolved on their master's work, their minds set on heaven, the warriors fought then.
The great chariot-warriors, loosing weapons of many forms, roaring at each other and striking each other,
Strike! Pierce! Seize! Hit! Cut!—such cries were heard in your and their forces.
Then Shalya, O great king, pierced the great chariot-warrior, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, with sharp arrows, wishing to kill him.
Partha, O great king, knowing vitals, laughing as it were, drove iron arrows at the great chariot-warrior's vitals.
Holding him off with arrows, the greatly renowned one, enraged, wishing to kill the Pandava, pierced him in the battle with many heron-feathered arrows.
Then again, O great king, he struck Yudhishthira in the sight of the whole army with a straight-jointed arrow.
The king of dharma, greatly renowned, also enraged, pierced the king of the Madras with sharp arrows feathered with heron plumes.
The great chariot-warrior pierced Chandrasena with seventy, his charioteer with nine, and Drumasena with sixty-four arrows.
When the wheel-guard had been slain by the great-souled Pandava, Shalya then killed twenty-five Chedis, O king.
He pierced Satyaki with twenty-five, Bhimasena with five, and both sons of Madri with a hundred sharp arrows in the battle.
As he thus ranged in battle, O best of kings, Partha (Yudhishthira) sent sharp arrows like venomous serpents.
With a broad-headed arrow Kunti's son Yudhishthira cut the tip of his banner from his chariot as he stood in front.
We saw his banner cut by the great-souled Pandava falling like a mountain peak struck.
Seeing his banner fallen and the Pandava standing, the king of the Madras became enraged and loosed a shower of arrows.
Shalya of immeasurable spirit, bull among kshatriyas, showered the kshatriya with showers of arrows like a rain-bearing cloud.
Having pierced Satyaki, Bhimasena and the two sons of Madri each with five, he tormented Yudhishthira.
Then a net of arrows spread over the two Pandavas; we saw, O great king, as if a net of clouds had risen.
Then Shalya, enraged in the battle, covered the quarters and intermediate quarters with straight-jointed arrows, the great chariot-warrior.
Then King Yudhishthira, tormented by the net of arrows, lost his vigour, like Jambha slain by the slayer of Vritra.
Seeing him alone tormented by many great chariot-warriors, a great cry of "Well done" arose, the siddhas were delighted, and the sages gathered said "Marvel!"
In the battle Bhimasena, piercing Shalya, a thorn in valour, with one arrow, pierced him again with seven.
Satyaki too, with a hundred, from desire to save the son of Dharma, covered the lord of the Madras and roared a lion-roar.
Nakula with five and Sahadeva with seven pierced him, and swiftly pierced him again with seven.
That hero, exerting himself in the battle, tormented by those great chariot-warriors, drawing his dreadful bow, swift and able to bear weight,
Shalya pierced Satyaki with twenty-five, O revered one, Bhimasena with seventy-three, and Nakula with seven.
Then, cutting the bow and arrow of the bowman Sahadeva in the battle with a broad-headed arrow, he pierced him with seventy-three.
Sahadeva, in the battle, taking another strung bow, struck his maternal uncle of great splendour with five arrows, blazing like fire, like venomous serpents.
Bhimasena with seventy-three, Satyaki with nine arrows, and the king of dharma with sixty went and pierced Shalya.
Then Shalya, O great king, pierced by those great chariot-warriors, streamed blood from his limbs like a mountain red ochre.
He swiftly pierced all those mighty archers with five arrows each, O king; it was as marvellous.
Then with another broad-headed arrow, O revered one, that great chariot-warrior cut the bow of the son of Dharma with its string in the battle.
Then, taking another bow, the great chariot-warrior son of Dharma covered Shalya with his chariot, horses, charioteer and banner with arrows.
Covered in the battle by the son of Dharma's arrows, he pierced Yudhishthira with ten sharp arrows.
Satyaki, then enraged on seeing the son of Dharma tormented by arrows, held back the brave lord of the Madras with floods of arrows.
He cut Satyaki's great bow with a razor-arrow, and struck those led by Bhimasena with three each.
Satyaki of true valour, enraged, O great king, hurled at him a javelin with a golden shaft, of great worth.
Bhimasena an iron arrow like a blazing serpent, Nakula a dart in the battle, Sahadeva a fair mace, and the king of dharma a shataghni, all wishing to kill Shalya in the fight.
As those five projectiles loosed from their arms came swiftly, Shalya cut the javelin sent by Satyaki with broad-headed arrows.
The gold-adorned arrow sent by Bhima he cut in two in the battle, the glorious skilled-handed one.
He warded off with floods of arrows the dart sent by Nakula, with a golden shaft, terrible, and the mace by Sahadeva.
And the king's shataghni with the arrow-wielder he cut, O Bharata; in the sight of the sons of Pandu, he roared a lion-roar; but Shaineya could not bear the foe's victory in battle.
Then, taking another bow, Satyaki, overcome with rage, pierced the lord of the Madras with two and his charioteer with three arrows.
Then Shalya, O great king, enraged, pierced all of them with ten arrows each, hard, like great elephants with goads.
Those great chariot-warriors, though held back in the battle by the king of the Madras, slayers of foes, could not stand before him.
Then King Duryodhana, seeing Shalya's valour, thought the Pandavas, Panchalas and Srinjayas slain.
Then, O king, the mighty-armed, glorious Bhimasena, giving up life in his mind, fought the lord of the Madras.
Nakula, Sahadeva and the great chariot-warrior Satyaki then surrounded Shalya and showered him with arrows on every side.
Surrounded by four mighty-bowed great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas, the glorious king of the Madras fought them.
The king of dharma, O king, with a razor-arrow in the great battle, swiftly slew the king of the Madras' wheel-guard.
When that brave great chariot-warrior wheel-guard was slain, the very strong king of the Madras strewed the soldiers with arrows.
Seeing those soldiers covered, O king, the king of dharma Yudhishthira thought in the battle:
How could that great word of Madhava not come true? For the enraged king would not destroy my army in battle.
Then the Pandavas, with chariots, elephants and horses, O elder brother, approached the lord of the Madras, pressing him from all sides.
That shower of weapons that rose, full of floods of weapons of many kinds, he scattered in the battle, O king, like wind great clouds.
Then we saw the golden-feathered shower of arrows hurled by Shalya, going through the sky like a swarm of locusts.
Those arrows sent by the king of the Madras at the head of the battle, falling, were seen like flights of locusts.
The sky became, as it were, uninterrupted, O lord of men, with the arrows loosed from the king of the Madras' bow, gold-adorned.
None of the Pandavas or of ours was seen there, when a great darkness of arrows was made in that great fear.
Seeing the ocean of the Pandava force churned by the strong king of the Madras through dexterity and showers of arrows, gods, gandharvas and danavas fell into utmost wonder.
He, tormenting them on every side with arrows, covered the king of dharma and roared repeatedly like a lion.
Covered by him in the battle, the great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas could not then confront that great chariot-warrior in the fight.
The chariot-warriors led by the king of dharma, with Bhimasena in front, did not abandon the brave Shalya, ornament of battle.
Likewise the others, the mighty archers, Dhananjaya, mighty-armed, again covered with showers of arrows, two each.
Studded with arrow-thorns, your men, O best of the Bharatas, did not leave Partha in the battle, though slain by sharp arrows.
Led by Drona's son, those great chariot-warriors fought Arjuna in the battle with a line of chariots, surrounding him.
The arrows they hurled, O king, adorned with gold, filled the seat of Arjuna's chariot swiftly.
The two Krishnas, mighty archers, bulls among all bowmen, delighted, arrogant in battle, looked at their limbs pierced by arrows.
The chariot-seat, wheels, pole, traces, yoke and its drag became then a mass of arrows.
We have never seen, O king, nor heard such as what your men did there to Partha.
That chariot shone on every side with sharp variegated-feathered arrows, like a celestial car blazing with hundreds of meteors on the earth.
Then Arjuna, O great king, with straight-jointed arrows covered that army, as a cloud with rain a mountain.
Being slain in the battle by arrows marked with Partha's name, the Parthas thought the world full of Partha, seeing it so.
Then the Partha fire, with marvellous flames of arrows and a great wind of bow-sound, swiftly burned your fuel of an army.
Of falling wheels and yokes on the ground, quivers, pennants, banners with chariots,
poles, drags, triple poles, axles, traces and goads, in every way,
of falling heads with earrings and turbans, of arms, O great king, and shoulders on every side,
parasols with fans and heaps of crowns were seen on the paths of Partha's chariot, O Bharata.
The earth became impassable, a mire of flesh and blood, O best of the Bharatas, like Rudra's playground, giving fear to the timid and joy to the brave.
Having slain in the battle two thousand armoured chariots, Partha shone, scorcher of foes, like a smokeless blazing fire.
As the Lord Fire, having burned the world of moving and unmoving, is seen smokeless, O king, so was the great chariot-warrior Partha.
Seeing the Pandava's prowess in the battle, Drona's son held back the Pandava with a chariot with many banners.
Those two tigers among men, white-horsed, best of bowmen, then quickly met, each wishing the other's death.
A most dreadful shower of arrows took place between them, O great king, like rain from clouds at the end of summer, O best of the Bharatas.
Rivals of each other, with straight-jointed arrows they hewed each other in the battle like two bulls with horns.
Their battle, O great king, was for a long time as if even, and a great dreadful meeting of weapons took place there.
Then Drona's son pierced Arjuna with twelve gold-feathered keen arrows and Vasudeva with ten, O Bharata.
Then Bibhatsu, laughing, twanged Gandiva, having honoured the preceptor's son for a moment in the great battle.
The great chariot-warrior Savyasachin made his chariot horseless and charioteerless, and gently pierced him with three arrows.
Standing on the chariot whose horses were slain, Drona's son hurled an iron pestle like an iron club at the son of Pandu.
As it suddenly came, adorned with plates of gold, the hero Partha, destroyer of foes, cut it into seven.
Seeing the pestle cut, Drona's son, exceedingly angry, took up a dreadful club like the peak of a king of mountains, and hurled it at Partha, Drona's son, skilled in war.
Seeing that club like Death enraged, the Pandava Arjuna quickly struck it with five of the best arrows.
Cut and fallen to the earth by Partha's arrows in the great battle, it split the hearts of kings of the earth with its sound, O Bharata.
Then the Pandava pierced Drona's son with three other arrows; deeply pierced by the strong Partha, the very mighty Drona's son was not bewildered, and stood in his own manliness.
Then Sudharma, O king, covered Bharadvaja's son, the great chariot-warrior, with masses of arrows in the sight of all kshatriyas.
Then Suratha too, great chariot-warrior of the Panchalas, rushed in the battle at Drona's son in a chariot with a cloud-like roar.
Drawing his excellent bow, firm, able to bear all burdens, he covered him with arrows like blazing venomous serpents.
Drona's son, enraged at Suratha the great chariot-warrior as he came, became like a serpent struck with a rod.
Making a three-lined frown, licking the corners of his mouth, looking at Suratha in rage and wiping his bowstring, he loosed a sharp iron arrow bright as Death's rod.
It pierced his heart and entered with great speed, splitting the earth's surface like Shakra's thunderbolt hurled.
Then he lay on the ground, struck by the iron arrow, like a peak of great worth of a mountain struck by thunderbolt.
When that hero was slain, the mighty Drona's son quickly mounted a chariot, that best of chariot-warriors.
Then, ready, O great king, Drona's son, arrogant in battle, fought Arjuna, surrounded by Samshaptakas, in the battle.
A great battle took place there between Arjuna and his foes, with the sun at midday, that increased Yama's realm.
We saw a marvel there, seeing their prowess, that Arjuna alone fought the heroes at once.
There was a great crush of Arjuna with the foes, as of old Shatakratu with the great daitya host.
Streams of arrows by the thousand flowed from those two, O great king, like streams of water on every side from clouds in due season.
The king pierced the Parshata with five iron arrows, and slayer of Drona, fierce-arrowed, pierced again with seven.
Dhrishtadyumna, strong, firm in valour, tormented Duryodhana in the battle with seventy arrows.
Seeing the king tormented, his brothers, O best of the Bharatas, with a great army surrounded the Parshata.
Surrounded by those brave atirathas on every side, he ranged in the battle, O king, showing dexterity of hand.
Shikhandin, joined with the Prabhadrakas, fought Kritavarman and Gautama, the great chariot-warrior, both bowmen.
There too a very great, dreadful battle took place, O lord of men, of those giving up life in a gamble of life.
Shalya, loosing showers of arrows in every quarter, tormented the Pandavas, with Satyaki and Vrikodara.
So too he fought both twins in the battle, equal in prowess to Yama, with valour and strength, O king of kings.
Of the Pandavas driven by Shalya's arrows in the great battle, none of the great chariot-warriors found a protector.
Then, when the king of dharma was harassed, the brave Nakula, Madri's delight, rushed with speed at his maternal uncle.
Covering Shalya in the battle, Nakula, slayer of heroes, pierced him in the chest with ten arrows, smiling.
With all-iron arrows polished by smiths, gold-feathered, stone-whetted, driven by the bow-machine,
Shalya, tormented by his own sister's son, the great soul, tormented Nakula, his sister's son, the great soul.
Then King Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Satyaki and Sahadeva son of Madri rushed at the king of the Madras.
As they swiftly came on, filling quarters and intermediate quarters with sound and shaking the earth, the commander, conqueror of foes, met them in the battle.
Having pierced Yudhishthira with three, Bhimasena with seven, Satyaki with a hundred in the battle, and Sahadeva with three arrows,
the lord of the Madras then, O revered one, with a razor-arrow cut the great-souled Nakula's bow with its arrow, and Shalya's cut bow shattered.
Then, taking another bow, the great chariot-warrior son of Madri quickly filled the king of the Madras' chariot with feathered arrows.
Yudhishthira and Sahadeva, O revered one, pierced the lord of the Madras in the chest with ten arrows each.
Then Bhimasena with sixty and Satyaki with nine arrows, rushing at the king of the Madras, struck him with heron-feathered arrows.
The king of the Madras, enraged, pierced Satyaki with nine arrows and again with seventy straight-jointed arrows.
Then he cut his bow with its arrow in his fist, O revered one, and sent his four horses to death in the battle.
Having made Satyaki chariotless, the mighty king of the Madras struck him on every side with a hundred arrows.
The two sons of Madri, enraged, pierced Bhimasena the Pandava and Yudhishthira, O Kaurava, with ten arrows.
There we saw the marvellous manliness of the king of the Madras, that the Parthas together did not prevail in the battle.
Then Satyaki of true valour, mounting another chariot and seeing the Pandavas tormented, come under the power of the king of the Madras, strong, rushed with speed at the lord of the Madras.
Shalya, ornament of battle, advanced against his coming chariot in his own chariot, like a rutting elephant against a rutting elephant.
A tumultuous encounter, wondrous to behold, took place between the hero Satyaki and the lord of the Madras, such as of old between Shambara and the king of the gods.
Seeing the king of the Madras standing in the battle, Satyaki pierced him with ten arrows and said, "Stand, stand!"
The king of the Madras, much pierced by that great soul, pierced Satyaki in return with sharp variegated-feathered arrows.
With bodies overcome by sleep, they sat down on the ground, firmly joined with fatigue and wounded by arrows of many kinds.
One who sees only the honey and not the fall, deprived by greed for honey, grieves exactly as you do.
'Having conquered in battle, I shall make peace with Yudhishthira, the son of Dharma, afterwards, with Keshava'—so he said.
[Arjunaka said:] "What fault is there in me, foolish one? Death compelled me, dependent and helpless, to do so."
Govinda, the affection you have for me is known to me; with friendship and love you have always been compassionate to me.
Then the high-minded Kaurava King Dhritarashtra gave great wealth in many forms to costly-worthy Brahmanas.
Great dreadful winds arose day by day, and many hair-raising portents for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas.
A dog alone followed the Pandavas as they set out into the forest; in order the heroes went to the Lauhitya, ocean of water.
Hearing my mother's words at the water-oblation, 'Let water be given to Karna'—I burn with that.
